questions.q: In the decision path taught in this lesson, what is the very first question to ask about a requirement?
options: Does it need Apex?
Does it only need to stop a bad save, with no data changes or routing?
Does it need a screen for the user?
Does it need a master-detail relationship?
questions.explain: The path starts with the narrowest, most restrictive tool: if the requirement is purely 'block a bad save,' a validation rule is the answer before considering anything more powerful.

questions.q: 'Require a reason when an Opportunity is marked Closed Lost' and 'When an Opportunity is marked Closed Lost, notify the sales manager and log a task' sound similar. Why do they resolve to different tools?
options: The first requirement is impossible to build declaratively
The first requirement requires Apex because it blocks a save
They actually use the exact same tool
The second requirement has a side effect (sending a notification, creating a record), which a validation rule cannot do — it can only block or allow
questions.explain: A validation rule can never create a record or send a notification — only allow or block the save. Any side effect pushes the requirement to Flow (or a legacy Workflow Rule).

questions.q: Which requirement is the best fit for a roll-up summary field?
options: Showing the total value of all open Opportunities on an Account, stored and kept current automatically
Displaying a Case's age in days
Requiring a Close Reason on lost Opportunities
Routing a Contract over $100,000 to a director for sign-off
questions.explain: A stored, automatically-maintained aggregate from direct child records is exactly what a roll-up summary field is built for.

questions.q: A nightly job needs to recalculate a complex loyalty-tier formula against 200,000 customer records, incorporating external data. Why does this point toward Apex rather than Flow?
options: Flow cannot run on a schedule at all
Apex is required for anything involving a formula
The combination of volume, complexity, and scale goes beyond what Flow can cleanly and efficiently express
Roll-up summary fields would be a better fit instead
questions.explain: The decision path's last step is Apex for genuinely bulk, transactional, or algorithmically complex logic beyond Flow's practical limits — this scenario is the textbook example.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the 'actual skill' when choosing automation tools for a real application?
options: Choosing the right tool per individual requirement, and letting several tools compose together (e.g. a roll-up feeding a validation rule's threshold)
Always defaulting to Apex for consistency
Finding the single tool that can handle the entire application by itself
Avoiding Flow entirely in favor of legacy Workflow Rules
questions.explain: Real applications typically combine several of the five declarative tools — the skill is matching each specific requirement to its right tool, not finding one tool to do everything.
